claims.text: The starting material is an as-cast refractory high-entropy alloy based on heavy refractory elements such as Nb, Mo, Ta, and W.
The starting alloy has a single-phase or dual-phase BCC/B2 structure.
The intervention replaces 5–10 at.% of the heavy refractory content with Al.
The Al-substituted alloy will have at least 20% greater creep strength at approximately 900°C than the baseline.
Replacing heavy refractory content with Al will reduce the alloy density.
The Al-substituted alloy will retain essentially unchanged room-temperature yield strength.
The Al-substituted alloy will retain essentially unchanged room-temperature ductility.
Al addition will produce a stable, refined phase distribution.
Al addition will improve grain-boundary characteristics.
A refined phase distribution and improved grain-boundary characteristics inhibit grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperature.
A refined phase distribution and improved grain-boundary characteristics inhibit dislocation mobility at elevated temperature.
Hindering grain-boundary sliding and dislocation motion improves high-temperature creep resistance.
Keeping Al incorporation within the proposed range avoids deleterious effects on the room-temperature strength–ductility balance.
An all-heavy-refractory baseline has high density.
Prior RHEA studies show that increasing Al content can decrease density and increase room-temperature specific yield strength.
The magnitude of the property changes may depend on composition and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The predicted comparison is described as being against an as-cast baseline, but the decisive experiment applies homogenization to both the baseline and Al-modified samples. The experimental control therefore is not strictly the stated as-cast baseline.
